title: Menaion: fixed feasts and saints, 1 September to 31 August
scope: Readings proper to fixed-date commemorations (date: month-day, on the church's calendar) and to the Saturdays and Sundays defined by dates around the great feasts (range: that weekday falling between from and to).
licence: Released with bible-rs under the MIT licence. The table holds Scripture references only: no Bible text and no prose from the sources. Notes are our own.
usage: Byzantine usage, Revised Julian fixed feasts, Julian Paschalion, in two usages: Greek (the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America as goarch.org prints it; the default) and Antiochian (the Antiochian Orthodox Christian Archdiocese of North America's service texts and charts). Where they differ both are recorded: a reading or an entry marked "in": "greek" or "antiochian" is read only in that usage, and an entry's "greek" or "antiochian" object changes its name, its rules (weekday, sunday, saturday, bright; none = no reading) or its confidence there. Slavic (OCA) and other alternatives (a patron's readings) are kept in 'variants' and 'slavic' and are never read.
numbering: English Bible (KJV/Hebrew) chapter and verse, the grid's numbering, with half-verse letters dropped. Each string in refs is one contiguous range ('Book C:V', 'Book C:V-V' or 'Book C:V-C:V', with the grid's book abbreviations); a reading's refs are read together, in order, as one lesson.
confidence: high: a source of the usage (the Antiochian service texts and charts; goarch.org) agrees with at least one independent source. medium: the sources differ (usually by a verse at the start or end) or the reference rests on one source. low: no Antiochian or Greek source was found, or the yearly ordo decides.

rules: weekday: what the entry does on a weekday. replaces = its Epistle and Gospel are read instead of the day's; epistle / gospel = only that one replaces the day's; own = the entry is the day (great feasts, eves, the Saturdays and Sundays around the feasts); optional = read only where the saint is kept (not shown by default).
sunday: feast = it replaces the Sunday readings; epistle = its Epistle with the Sunday Gospel; sunday = the Sunday readings only; special = see the note.
matins_on_sunday: feast = the feast's Matins Gospel replaces the Sunday eothinon (the Twelve Great Feasts).

Saturdays follow the weekday rule. On a Saturday with its own readings (before or after the Elevation, the Nativity and Theophany) a saint yields unless saturday says otherwise: epistle = its Epistle with the Saturday's Gospel; gospel = the Saturday's Epistle with its Gospel. On a Sunday with its own readings the sunday rule applies as on any Sunday.
Vespers readings belong to the Great Vespers served the evening before the date (on the eves of the Nativity and Theophany, the Vespers joined to the Liturgy).

In Great Lent only the Annunciation, the Forty Martyrs and the Finding of the Forerunner's Head are read on weekdays; in Holy Week and on Pascha only the Annunciation. In Bright Week only an entry with bright reads: on its own day only that reading (Epistle or Gospel) with the day's other; moved into Bright Week, in Antiochian usage its Epistle with the day's Gospel, in Greek usage still its bright reading. St George moves to Bright Monday when 23 April falls on or before Pascha; the other bright entries that fall from Palm Sunday to Pascha move to the next Bright Week days.

Days that keep their own readings: a great feast (own) on Pascha, in Holy Week, on Pentecost or in Bright Week is shown beside the day's readings at low confidence. On the Ascension only Sts Constantine and Helen give their Epistle. All Saints Sunday and the Monday of the Holy Spirit keep their Epistle: a feast gives only its Gospel. The leave-takings of Pascha and of Pentecost keep both readings unless a great feast falls. On St Theodore's and the Ascetics' Saturdays a saint with sunday epistle gives, in Antiochian usage, its Gospel with the commemoration's Epistle; in Greek usage both its readings. A saint falling on a Saturday of Souls (Meatfare, before Pentecost) is read the day before (in Greek usage only one with a Matins Gospel of its own; another yields); a great feast stays on its day and replaces the Saturday's readings. In Greek usage a saint with a Matins Gospel of its own falling on the Ascension is read the day after (except Sts Constantine and Helen), an entry with weekday gospel yields from Pascha to the leave-taking of Pentecost, and St Mark yields on a weekday of that season.
